claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Solution annealing or full homogenization produces a single-phase FCC Co-free FeNiCrMn microstructure with minimal second phases.
Local dynamic strain aging is the primary mechanism governing the dynamic behavior of Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Temperature- and strain-rate-dependent solute–dislocation interactions produce time-dependent dislocation pinning.
Time-dependent dislocation pinning causes serrated flow over an intermediate temperature–strain-rate regime.
Transient Mn-rich Cottrell atmospheres form during deformation in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Short-range ordering dynamically locks dislocations in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Changing temperature and strain rate changes solute diffusion sufficiently to permit or hinder the pinning of moving dislocations.
Dynamic strain aging alters strain-hardening behavior.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have comparable or slightly higher strain-rate sensitivity.
Serrated flow in Co-free FeNiCrMn will be most pronounced at intermediate temperatures.
At lower temperatures or significantly higher strain rates, cross-slip or mechanical twinning will take precedence over dynamic strain aging.
The increased importance of cross-slip or twinning will diminish or eliminate serrated flow.
Co is partially replaced by Fe to create the Co-free FeNiCrMn variant from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed phenomenon is most prominent in single-phase as-cast or homogenized material at strain rates up to about 10^3 s^-1.
At much higher temperatures, creep may overshadow dynamic strain aging.
At extremely low temperatures, athermal deformation processes may overshadow dynamic strain aging.
Comparable grain size, texture, and composition are required to isolate temperature and strain-rate effects in the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The material is described as Co-free, but the baseline field says Co is only partially replaced by Fe; partial replacement would ordinarily leave residual Co.

The design describes Hopkinson-bar tests across the full 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 range, although conventional Hopkinson-bar testing does not provide the quasi-static 10^-3 s^-1 portion; a separate quasi-static apparatus would be required.
